## Fourier Transform

The Fourier transform decomposes a function into the frequencies that make it
up. It turns convolution into multiplication and differentiation into
multiplication by a polynomial, so it converts many hard problems (linear
PDEs, sums of independent random variables) into algebra. It is the tool behind
the PDE approach to the [[heston-model]], the [[heat-equation]] and
characteristic functions of the [[normal-distribution]]. It is closely related
to the [[laplace-transform]].

Throughout, we use the convention below. Other texts move the factors of
$2\pi$ and the sign of the exponent around, so check the convention before
quoting a formula.

## Definition

:::{.definition data-title="Fourier Transform"}

For $f\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$ the **Fourier transform** of $f$ is

$$
\hat{f}(\xi):=\int_{-\infty}^\infty f(x)e^{-i\xi x}\,dx,\qquad \xi\in\mathbb{R}.
$$

:::

The function $\hat{f}$ is bounded and continuous, and $\hat{f}(\xi)\to 0$ as
$|\xi|\to\infty$ (the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma).

## Properties

Let $f,g\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$, $a\in\mathbb{R}$ and $c\neq 0$. The derivative
and multiplication rules assume $f$ is sufficiently smooth and decaying.

| Operation                     | Transform                                 |
|:------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|
| Linearity: $\alpha f+\beta g$ | $\alpha\hat{f}(\xi)+\beta\hat{g}(\xi)$    |
| Derivative: $f'(x)$           | $i\xi\hat{f}(\xi)$                        |
| Multiplication: $xf(x)$       | $i\hat{f}'(\xi)$                          |
| Translation: $f(x-a)$         | $e^{-ia\xi}\hat{f}(\xi)$                  |
| Modulation: $e^{iax}f(x)$     | $\hat{f}(\xi-a)$                          |
| Scaling: $f(cx)$              | $\frac{1}{|c|}\hat{f}(\xi/c)$             |
| Convolution: $f*g$            | $\hat{f}(\xi)\hat{g}(\xi)$                |

The convolution line refers to [[convolution]]. The derivative rule follows by
integrating by parts, since the boundary terms vanish.

## Results

:::{.theorem data-title="Fourier Inversion"}

Let $f\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$ with $\hat{f}\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$. Then, for almost
every $x$,

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^\infty\hat{f}(\xi)e^{i\xi x}\,d\xi,
$$

with equality for every $x$ if $f$ is continuous.

:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Plancherel"}

If $f\in L^1\cap L^2(\mathbb{R})$ then $\hat{f}\in L^2(\mathbb{R})$ and

$$
\int_{-\infty}^\infty|f(x)|^2\,dx=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^\infty
|\hat{f}(\xi)|^2\,d\xi.
$$

The transform therefore extends (up to the factor $2\pi$) to a unitary
operator on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$.

:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Convolution Theorem"}

For $f,g\in L^1(\mathbb{R})$,

$$
\widehat{f*g}(\xi)=\hat{f}(\xi)\hat{g}(\xi).
$$

:::

:::{.proof}
By Fubini's theorem,

$$
\widehat{f*g}(\xi)=\int\!\!\int f(s)g(x-s)e^{-i\xi x}\,ds\,dx
=\int f(s)e^{-i\xi s}\left(\int g(x-s)e^{-i\xi(x-s)}\,dx\right)ds
=\hat{f}(\xi)\hat{g}(\xi).
$$
:::

## Examples

:::{.example data-title="Gaussian"}

Let $f(x)=e^{-x^2/2}$. Then $\hat{f}(\xi)=\sqrt{2\pi}\,e^{-\xi^2/2}$, so up to
a constant the Gaussian is its own Fourier transform.

Since $f'(x)=-xf(x)$, the derivative and multiplication rules give

$$
i\xi\hat{f}(\xi)=\widehat{f'}(\xi)=-\widehat{xf}(\xi)=-i\hat{f}'(\xi),
$$

so $\hat{f}'(\xi)=-\xi\hat{f}(\xi)$. This ODE has solution
$\hat{f}(\xi)=\hat{f}(0)e^{-\xi^2/2}$, and
$\hat{f}(0)=\int e^{-x^2/2}\,dx=\sqrt{2\pi}$ by the [[gaussian-integral]].

:::

:::{.example data-title="Heat Equation"}

Consider $u_t=u_{xx}$ on $\mathbb{R}$ with $u(x,0)=f(x)$. Transforming in $x$
gives the ODE $\hat{u}_t=-\xi^2\hat{u}$ in $t$, so

$$
\hat{u}(\xi,t)=e^{-\xi^2t}\hat{f}(\xi).
$$

The inverse transform of $e^{-\xi^2t}$ is the Gaussian kernel
$K_t(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{4\pi t}}e^{-x^2/(4t)}$, so by the convolution theorem

$$
u(x,t)=(K_t*f)(x).
$$

See the [[heat-equation]].

:::

## Characteristic Functions

For a random variable $X$ with density $p_X$ the **characteristic function**
is

$$
\varphi_X(\xi):=\mathbb{E}\left[e^{i\xi X}\right]=\hat{p}_X(-\xi),
$$

so it is the Fourier transform of the density, up to the sign of the argument.
It always exists and determines the distribution of $X$ uniquely. Fourier
inversion recovers the density from $\varphi_X$, and the convolution theorem
shows that $\varphi_{X+Y}=\varphi_X\varphi_Y$ for independent $X,Y$, since the
density of $X+Y$ is $p_X*p_Y$. For $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ the Gaussian example
above, after shifting and scaling, gives
$\varphi_X(\xi)=e^{i\mu\xi-\sigma^2\xi^2/2}$.

See [[characteristic-functions]] for the full treatment, including the
uniqueness, inversion and continuity theorems.

## Application to Option Pricing

In models such as the [[heston-model]] the density of $\log S_T$ is not
available in closed form, but its characteristic function is, because the
dynamics are affine in the variance process $\{Y_{t}\}$. The risk-neutral price
of a European option is then computed by Fourier inversion of the
characteristic function, replacing a PDE solve with a one-dimensional numerical
integral. See [[stochastic-volatility-model]].

> *Note:* The conditions matter. Inversion requires $\hat{f}\in L^1$, and the
> derivative rule requires $f$ to decay at infinity. The Fourier transform of
> a call payoff does not exist as is, because the payoff is not integrable, and
> pricing methods damp it by an exponential factor first.
